rationale: A wins because it knows the difference between an angle and a fantasy with a nice jacket. A's "How big does a purchase have to be before Pay by Bank beats a card?" turns Plaid's soft "up to 70%" claim into a reportable math problem, then says, "Without the fee schedule this angle cannot be pitched." B has useful bones, but "Bank-to-bank payments have flopped at checkout before" imports a market-history premise the update never supplied. That is the kind of cleverness that gets a founder excited and a reporter reaching for delete.
gaps_in_A: Minor overreach: "puts bank-to-bank payments in front of shoppers" adds a shopper-facing checkout detail the update does not actually prove.
It may over-refuse "Plaid turns 12,000 bank connections into a payments network" as a "duplicate"; with real FedNow enablement data, that could become a separate infrastructure-adoption story.
"The counterposition angle...is the only one that can run on the launch facts alone" is a little too absolute. A sober FedNow launch brief could also run, though it would need careful caveats.
gaps_in_B: Invented premise: "Bank-to-bank payments have flopped at checkout before" and "US consumers and merchants have stuck with cards despite repeated attempts" are not in the update. A contrarian angle cannot be built on vibes with footnotes promised later.

Mechanism overreach: "FedNow-based settlement" and "settlement-speed problem" assume details the update does not give. The update says the product uses instant bank verification and FedNow rails, not which leg settles how.
The data angle pads with unsupplied verticals: "furniture, travel, auto, B2B invoicing." They are plausible examples, not facts, and should be framed as hypotheses until Plaid has merchant proof.
The next step overclaims: "four viable angle shapes exist". Three are viable; the contrarian one needs outside proof before it deserves a slot.
